title: Why we dwell in a sukkah
bullets: Remember the protection given during the Exodus.
Intend to fulfil the mitzvah when dwelling in the sukkah.
Begin practical preparations promptly after Yom Kippur.
parallel: Turn your chosen identity into a visible preparation.
narration: The sukkah recalls protection during the Exodus. Connect this intention to one concrete preparation, so your identity becomes an action.

title: Keep the roof under open sky
bullets: A building roof or tree above the sukkah can invalidate it.
Tree branches and mixed coverings require detailed evaluation.
Retractable roofs must be properly opened for dwelling.
parallel: Make the correct location your default before building.
narration: A sukkah needs the right exposure to the sky. Check overhead obstacles first; design your environment before relying on willpower.

title: Avoid an intervening canopy
bullets: A bed or canopy can create a separate covering below the roof.
Height, width and whether a canopy is fixed affect the ruling.
Do not assume every tent inside a sukkah is acceptable.
parallel: Remove an obstacle before it repeatedly interrupts the mitzvah.
narration: An intervening canopy can prevent valid sukkah dwelling. Remove the obstacle in advance, like removing a cue that repeatedly disrupts a useful routine.

title: Check stacked and mobile structures
bullets: A sukkah underneath another sukkah has special validity rules.
A mobile sukkah must withstand an ordinary wind.
Access involving a tree or animal has festival restrictions.
parallel: Choose a workable setting instead of forcing an unsuitable one.
narration: Stacked or mobile sukkahs have special conditions. Choose a suitable setup, just as useful habits need an environment that fits their purpose.

title: Choose valid roof materials
bullets: Roof covering must be detached plant material.
It must not be susceptible to ritual impurity; processed objects need examination.
Mats, planks, bundles and supports have additional rules.
parallel: Buy appropriate materials early and remove setup friction.
narration: Sukkah roof covering must be suitable detached plant material. Prepare approved materials early; reducing friction helps preparation, but never replaces the legal requirements.

title: Build stable, valid walls
bullets: Walls may use materials that cannot be used for the roof.
The minimum two-and-a-partial-third configuration has precise conditions.
Three complete stable walls simplify many practical questions.
parallel: Arrange a competent inspection partner and a concrete check-in.
narration: Sukkah walls must meet stability and layout requirements. Arrange a knowledgeable inspection partner; clear accountability helps you notice problems before the festival.

title: Create the required shade
bullets: At roof level, shade must exceed sunlight.
Holes, uneven roof surfaces and dangling branches have further conditions.
Prefer comfortable shade without making a permanent rainproof ceiling.
parallel: Observe the actual result instead of guessing.
narration: The roof must provide more shade than sunlight. Inspect what is really there; awareness comes before adjustment, just as noticing a routine comes before changing it.

title: Measure gaps and invalid covering
bullets: Air gaps and invalid roof materials have different limits.
Their position can change whether the whole sukkah remains valid.
Do not treat a simple gap measurement as a full validity certificate.
parallel: Review weak points with a precise checklist.
narration: Roof gaps and invalid materials have different rules. Review the weak points carefully; a useful checklist supports attention without deciding complex legal cases for you.

title: Respect the height boundaries
bullets: Minimum interior height is ten tefachim.
Height above twenty amot is invalid.
Raising floors or lowering coverings involves detailed conditions.
parallel: Make a correct measurement before locking in the structure.
narration: A sukkah has minimum and maximum height limits. Measure before construction choices become fixed; a good commitment prevents avoidable work later.

title: Leave enough usable space
bullets: The sukkah must contain at least seven by seven tefachim.
Rounded shapes must contain the required square area.
Keep the table in the sukkah rather than eating toward a table outside.
parallel: A tiny starting task is helpful; a tiny invalid sukkah is not.
narration: A sukkah needs the required usable space. Start preparation with one small task, but never shrink a religious requirement to fit the two-minute habit rule.

title: Create the roof through a valid act
bullets: A shelter built for shade can be suitable even without festival-specific intent.
A structure that simply becomes covered by itself can be invalid.
Carving space in a haystack needs the construction conditions in the source.
parallel: Perform the real preparatory action instead of only planning it.
narration: The roof must result from a valid act of making. Perform the actual preparation; planning alone cannot replace action, either in habit practice or construction.

title: Renew an existing sukkah
bullets: An older sukkah has rules concerning renewal for the festival.
The source describes renewing even a small roof area.
Festival-specific construction intention affects the older-sukkah case.
parallel: Make one real improvement to a setup you already have.
narration: An existing sukkah can call for renewal for the festival. Make a real, small improvement; steady useful action often matters more than rebuilding everything.

title: Borrow respectfully; never steal
bullets: A borrowed sukkah can fulfil the mitzvah.
Stolen materials and unauthorized use require distinct legal analysis.
If necessary, a sukkah can be built during permitted Chol HaMoed work.
parallel: Use supportive community access with clear permission.
narration: A borrowed sukkah can serve the mitzvah. Ask permission clearly and use community support; belonging helps practice, while ownership rights still matter.

title: Respect dedicated materials
bullets: Sukkah wood and decorations become restricted for ordinary use.
Duration and conditions differ between materials and festival settings.
Do not casually remove or repurpose decorations during the festival.
parallel: Store ordinary substitutes separately to avoid temptation.
narration: Dedicated sukkah materials have restrictions on ordinary use. Keep other supplies nearby; removing tempting shortcuts makes it easier to respect what has been set aside.

title: Make the sukkah your dwelling
bullets: Required meals and sleep belong in the sukkah, subject to exemptions.
The first night has a special bread obligation; amounts and rain need care.
Meal thresholds, blessings and sleeping customs need your community guidance.
parallel: Attach the meal routine to moving into the sukkah.
narration: Dwelling in the sukkah includes required meals and sleep, subject to exemptions. Link your meal preparation to entering the sukkah, creating a reliable cue for the mitzvah.

title: Understand obligations and exemptions
bullets: Women are exempt from obligatory sukkah dwelling but may participate.
Children require age-appropriate education; illness and genuine distress can exempt.
Travel, essential duties and caregivers have conditions, not blanket exemptions.
parallel: Fit preparation to real circumstances rather than manufacturing an exemption.
narration: Illness and genuine distress can create exemptions from sukkah dwelling. Adapt preparation to real circumstances; habit design must respect the law, not invent an exemption.

title: Separate building from its blessings
bullets: No construction blessing is normally recited for building the sukkah.
Shehecheyanu is generally included in festival Kiddush.
Building for someone else and unusual timing have further details.
parallel: Enjoy completing preparation without inventing a religious formula.
narration: Building the sukkah does not require inventing a construction blessing. Enjoy finishing preparation; an immediate positive feeling can encourage action without creating a new religious practice.

title: Follow the Shabbat prayer framework
bullets: When the first festival night is Shabbat, prayer has special wording.
The seven-blessing summary follows the Shabbat conclusion in this chapter.
Use the correct communal siddur and prayer setting.
parallel: Use an established group routine rather than improvising.
narration: When the festival begins on Shabbat, the prayer framework matters. Follow the correct community text; a supportive group can help a routine stay accurate.

title: Prepare the Kiddush sequence
bullets: The first-night sequence includes wine, festival sanctification, sukkah and time.
Standing and sitting customs differ between authorities.
Use your tradition’s siddur for the exact sequence and text.
parallel: Make the next step visible in the correct sequence.
narration: The first-night Kiddush has an ordered sequence. Prepare the correct siddur beforehand; a clear cue and response reduce confusion without changing the ritual.

title: Place the four species in the morning service
bullets: The morning service includes taking the species and full Hallel.
The source describes the festival service and blessing traditions.
Taking the species is omitted on Shabbat, even when Hallel is said.
parallel: Connect preparation to a reliable morning anchor.
narration: Taking the four species fits into the morning service, except on Shabbat. Use a reliable morning anchor to remember the preparation and the day-specific rules.

title: Inspect the lulav carefully
bullets: Inspect the central leaf, spine, top and condition of the leaves.
Splitting, severing, bending and dryness have distinct rules.
A borderline lulav needs knowledgeable inspection, not a picture-only verdict.
parallel: Review quality instead of counting possession as completion.
narration: A lulav needs careful inspection for specific defects. Review quality, not just ownership; repeating a checklist helps notice mistakes that automatic confidence can hide.

title: Identify a suitable myrtle branch
bullets: A valid hadas normally has three leaves emerging at one level.
Density along the required length and leaf loss matter.
Berries, dryness and a cut top have additional conditions.
parallel: Look closely at the defining feature before choosing.
narration: A myrtle branch has specific leaf-pattern requirements. Notice the actual structure before choosing; careful observation is more useful than assuming that every green branch qualifies.

title: Identify the willow species
bullets: The willow has identifying leaf and stem characteristics.
A similar-looking alternative species may be invalid.
Dryness, loss of leaves and a cut tip can invalidate a branch.
parallel: Satisfy the real need with the correct item, not a tempting look-alike.
narration: The mitzvah requires the correct willow species and condition. Identify what is actually needed; an appealing substitute does not become valid simply because it is convenient.

title: Examine the etrog and its provenance
bullets: Check dryness, missing material, the top, stem, stains and shape.
A naturally absent pitam differs from one that broke off.
Minimum size is an egg’s volume; grafting requires reliable provenance.
parallel: Learn one inspection skill at a time without overlooking validity.
narration: An etrog has rules about defects and reliable provenance. Learn its inspection carefully, one skill at a time; gradual learning never excuses using an invalid specimen.

title: Distinguish first-day and later-day defects
bullets: Stolen species are unacceptable; acquisition details need careful review.
Some defects differ between the first day and later days.
Sephardic and Ashkenazic rulings differ on several invalidities.
parallel: Recheck the context rather than applying yesterday’s rule automatically.
narration: Some four-species defects have different first-day and later-day rules. Review the context instead of repeating yesterday’s judgment automatically; correct practice includes thoughtful reassessment.

title: Check the species measurements
bullets: The lulav spine requires four tefachim.
Myrtle and willow require three tefachim.
The lulav spine must extend above the other branches; measurement traditions differ.
parallel: Prepare a suitable measuring tool before shopping.
narration: The species have minimum measurements in tefachim. Prepare an appropriate measuring tool before shopping; deciding in advance reduces friction while preserving the actual requirement.

title: Take all four species correctly
bullets: Use one lulav, three myrtle branches, two willow branches and one etrog.
Take them in their growth orientation; bless before completing the act.
Handedness, binding, shaking order and interpositions have tradition-specific details.
parallel: Practise the sequence before the festival; the complete mitzvah remains required.
narration: All four species belong in the mitzvah, with the correct arrangement and orientation. Practise the sequence beforehand; rehearsal helps, but never replaces the complete required act.

title: Use the daytime opportunity
bullets: Taking the species is a daytime mitzvah.
The whole day is available; prompt performance is preferred.
A missed morning can be recovered later that day.
parallel: Use a morning cue and a same-day recovery reminder.
narration: Taking the four species is a daytime mitzvah. Set a morning cue and a same-day recovery reminder, so a missed first opportunity does not become a missed day.

title: Respect designated fragrance use
bullets: Myrtle designated for the mitzvah must not be used for smelling.
Avoid smelling the mitzvah etrog because of the blessing dispute.
Designation and preparation affect which restrictions apply.
parallel: Keep a separate fragrance available instead of using a restricted shortcut.
narration: The mitzvah myrtle has restrictions on fragrance use. Keep a separate alternative nearby; removing an unnecessary temptation makes respectful practice easier.

title: Keep the species fresh correctly
bullets: The source permits returning the lulav to water on Yom Tov.
Adding water and replacing water have different festival rules.
Chol HaMoed allows the appropriate freshness routine.
parallel: Prepare storage and an allowed care checklist in advance.
narration: Caring for the species has festival-specific rules. Prepare storage and an allowed care checklist; reducing setup effort supports care without making every maintenance action permitted.

title: Plan transport before the festival
bullets: Species brought from beyond the festival boundary have a specific case ruling.
Permission for the item does not permit every transport instruction.
Asking someone to do prohibited work requires separate evaluation.
parallel: Set logistics beforehand rather than improvising an unlawful shortcut.
narration: Transport has festival restrictions even when a brought item can be used. Plan logistics beforehand; commitment devices should prevent rushed shortcuts, not authorize prohibited work.

title: Balance beauty and resources
bullets: Beautifying a mitzvah can require additional expenditure within defined limits.
The one-third rule has details concerning what is compared.
Resources and obligation affect the practical financial ruling.
parallel: Make the preparation appealing within a responsible budget.
narration: Beautifying the mitzvah has defined financial rules. Make preparation appealing within a responsible budget; attractiveness supports effort without turning every enhancement into an unlimited obligation.

title: Teach children through real practice
bullets: A child able to perform the shaking receives practical mitzvah education.
Give age-appropriate instruction and suitable species access.
First-day ownership must be handled carefully before giving a set to a child.
parallel: Begin instruction with one manageable rehearsal, then teach the whole act.
narration: Children learn the mitzvah through suitable practice. Begin teaching with a manageable rehearsal, then teach the complete act; a small learning step does not reduce the mitzvah.

title: Ownership and the Shabbat exception
bullets: Do not take the four species on Shabbat.
First-day fulfilment requires ownership, not an ordinary loan.
A conditional gift works only if its return conditions are fulfilled.
parallel: Use a clear agreement and check the festival calendar.
narration: The four species are not taken on Shabbat. First-day ownership also matters; use a clear agreement and calendar check, rather than treating possession as enough.

title: Use the correct festival Torah readings
bullets: The chapter specifies the festival Torah readings and maftir.
The schedule follows the festival and location.
Use the local synagogue’s calendar rather than extrapolating from another place.
parallel: Keep the correct calendar where it will be used.
narration: Festival Torah readings follow the correct day and location. Keep the local calendar visible; a well-placed cue makes accuracy easier during a busy week.

title: Follow the Hoshanot custom
bullets: The chapter describes daily circling and seven circuits on the seventh day.
Shabbat, possession of species and mourning affect participation customs.
Follow the synagogue’s order and do not invent a universal arrangement.
parallel: Let a knowledgeable community guide a shared routine.
narration: Hoshanot has day-specific practices and community customs. Join the correct local order; a supportive group helps participation without erasing differences between traditions.

title: Notice the second-night difference
bullets: This chapter addresses the second festival night in the Diaspora.
Its Kiddush sequence differs from the first-night sequence.
Israel does not observe a second Sukkot festival day in the same way.
parallel: Observe which day and location you are in before acting.
narration: The second festival night has a different Kiddush context in the Diaspora. Notice the day and location before acting; awareness prevents copying the wrong routine.

title: Continue without repeating every first-day blessing
bullets: The taking blessing continues on eligible festival days.
Shehecheyanu is not repeated routinely for the species on day two.
If day one was Shabbat, the first actual taking has its own blessing sequence.
parallel: Track completion accurately while respecting each day’s conditions.
narration: Festival practice continues, but first-time blessings are not repeated automatically. Track the actual completed action and the day’s conditions, rather than confusing a streak with correct practice.

title: Follow the Chol HaMoed reading schedule
bullets: The Torah-reading order follows the current festival day.
Israel and Diaspora reading arrangements differ.
Shabbat Chol HaMoed has a distinct reading and haftarah.
parallel: Place a correct day-by-day reference beside the routine.
narration: Chol HaMoed readings depend on the day and location. Place the correct reference beside your routine; environment design helps prevent an automatic but inaccurate choice.

title: Prepare separately for Hoshana Rabbah
bullets: Hoshana Rabbah has additional prayer and willow customs.
The separate willow practice has no blessing.
Arrange appropriate branches and follow your community’s handling and disposal customs.
parallel: Prepare the materials and enjoy completion without inventing a reward ritual.
narration: Hoshana Rabbah has a separate willow custom without a blessing. Prepare suitable branches in advance; a satisfying finish can support preparation without inventing a new religious ritual.
